claims.text: The feedstock is pre-alloyed AlCrFeNiSi powder with a particle-size distribution typical of metallic additive manufacturing.
Conventional laser- or electron-beam melting imposes a high thermal load on AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing generates large thermal gradients.
Large thermal gradients in conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing produce residual stresses and associated mechanical-property degradation.
Binder jetting followed by controlled sub-melting-point sintering and HIP constitutes a lower-energy processing route than conventional laser- or electron-beam melting.
Reduced heat input minimizes steep thermal gradients in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Minimizing steep thermal gradients lowers residual stresses.
Reduced heat input prevents the formation of thermal defects.
Low-energy sintering produces a more uniform microstructure with minimized phase disproportionation.
HIP densifies the sintered AlCrFeNiSi material.
HIP improves interparticle bonding after low-temperature sintering.
Improved densification and interparticle bonding enhance mechanical properties relative to conventional high-thermal-load processing.
Low-energy sintering followed by HIP will significantly reduce residual stresses relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Low-energy sintering followed by HIP will improve mechanical strength relative to conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Low-energy sintering followed by HIP will yield a more uniform microstructure than conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
The resulting miniature components will provide performance comparable or superior to conventionally additively manufactured components.
The proposed effect may not extend to larger or more complex geometries or to different powder compositions.
